text:
Juno was the first spacecraft to reach Jupiter on solar power, with wings large enough to work at five times Earth's distance from the Sun. Its electronics ride in a titanium vault, shielded from Jupiter's radiation. It also carried three small LEGO figures.

In May 2012, Dragon became the first commercial spacecraft to visit the International Space Station. Astronaut Don Pettit caught it with the station's robot arm. It was the first American spacecraft at the station since the Shuttle retired, and it led to twenty Dragon supply runs, and to Crew Dragon.

In 2014, India's Mungal-yaan reached Mars orbit on its first try, making India the first Asian country to get there. It was built quickly and cheaply, for about seventy-three million dollars. Planned to last six months, it worked for seven and a half years.

Japan's Hayabusa 2 blasted a crater in the asteroid Ryugu with a copper projectile, then touched down to collect fresh rock from below the surface. Its capsule landed in the Australian outback with five point four grams of the asteroid. The spacecraft flew on, toward another asteroid it should reach in 2031.

Osiris Rex orbited the asteroid Bennu just one point seven five kilometers up, closer than any spacecraft has orbited anything. It touched the surface to grab a sample, and in 2023 its capsule landed in Utah with a hundred and twenty-one grams of asteroid. In it were fourteen of the twenty amino acids that make up proteins.

Falcon Heavy is three Falcon 9 first stages side by side. On its first flight, it sent a red Tesla Roadster into orbit around the Sun, and its two side boosters flew back and landed next to each other at Cape Canaveral.

In-Sight listened to Mars. Its seismometer recorded marsquakes, showing that the planet's interior is still active, and measured its core, about half the size of Earth's. Dust slowly covered its solar panels, and it fell silent in December 2022.

The Parker Solar Probe is the first spacecraft to fly through the Sun's outer atmosphere. Its carbon heat shield keeps the instruments behind it cool. At its closest, about six million kilometers from the Sun, it travels at six hundred and ninety thousand kilometers an hour, the fastest object people have ever made.

In January 2019, China's Chahng-uh 4 made the first landing on the far side of the Moon. Because the Moon blocks any direct radio link with Earth, China first placed a relay satellite beyond it. The rover, Yoo-too 2, drove for years across the floor of the Moon's largest and oldest crater.

In May 2019, SpaceX launched its first sixty Starlink satellites, flat-packed and stacked on a single rocket. Watch them string out along their orbit. Today, more than eleven thousand are in orbit, about a third of everything up there.

In May 2020, Crew Dragon became the first spacecraft built by a private company to carry astronauts into orbit, and the first crew launch from American soil since the last Shuttle flew, in 2011. Its capsules land under parachutes at sea, and fly again.

China's first Mars mission, Tyen-wen One, sent an orbiter, a lander and a rover together. In May 2021, China became the first country to land and drive on Mars at its first attempt. The rover, Joo-rong, drove almost two kilometers, then went into hibernation for the Martian winter, and never woke up.

Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater on Mars in February 2021, to look for signs of ancient life in an old river delta. It carried Ingenuity, a small helicopter that made the first powered flight on another planet, and flew seventy-two times. The rover seals rock samples in tubes, for a future mission to bring home.

Tyen-huh is the core of Tyen-gong, China's own space station. Two laboratory modules joined it in 2022, and crews of three have lived aboard ever since. The rocket's twenty-one-ton core stage reached orbit too, and fell back uncontrolled ten days later.

November 2021. Russia destroys one of its own dead satellites with a missile. Hours later, the seven people aboard the International Space Station shelter in their capsules as the station passes near the cloud. This time the debris was low enough to feel the thin upper air, and almost all of it fell back within three years.

Dart was the first test of defending the Earth by knocking an asteroid off course. In September 2022, it steered itself head-on into Dye-morphos, a moonlet a hundred and sixty meters wide. The hit shortened Dye-morphos's orbit by thirty-two minutes. Seventy-three seconds would have counted as a success.

On Christmas Day 2021, the James Webb Space Telescope launched folded inside an Ariane 5, and unfolded on its way to a point one and a half million kilometers from Earth. Its gold mirror is six and a half meters across. It sees galaxies from the first few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

Starlink's second generation is more than twice as heavy as the first, with about four times the capacity, and lasers that link each satellite to its neighbors. Since 2024, some of them also work as cell towers in orbit, sending texts straight to ordinary phones.

In August 2023, India's Chundra-yaan 3 landed near the Moon's south pole, where ice may hide in shadowed craters. India became the fourth country to land softly on the Moon, and the first to land near its south pole. Its little rover, Prag-yaan, drove about a hundred meters before the long lunar night.

In January 2025, Blue Origin's New Glenn, named after John Glenn, reached orbit on its first flight. On its second, its booster landed on a ship at sea, while the rocket sent two NASA probes on their way to Mars.

Amazon's answer to Starlink began as Project Kyper, and is now called Amazon Leo. Its first twenty-seven production satellites went up in April 2025, on an Atlas Five. More than three thousand are planned.

In April 2026, four astronauts became the first people to fly to the Moon since 1972. Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Cook and Jeremy Hansen looped around the far side of the Moon in an Orion capsule, and went farther from Earth than anyone ever had.

And in September 2026, on its fourteenth flight, Starship reached orbit for the first time. It is the largest and most powerful rocket ever flown, built from stainless steel, and its booster can be caught out of the air by the arms of its launch tower.

This is where we are now. Almost thirty-four thousand objects are in orbit. More than eleven thousand of them are Starlink satellites.

And a great deal of it is junk. More than fourteen thousand of the objects in orbit, over four in every ten, are spent rocket stages, parts thrown off during launches, and debris from explosions and collisions. Many of the satellites are dead too. And these are only the pieces big enough to track. Below that, there are about one and a half million fragments between one and ten centimeters across, and at these speeds, even a one-centimeter fragment can disable a satellite. Low pieces fall back within a few years. Above about eight hundred kilometers, they can stay up for centuries.

Who put it all there? For decades, the Soviet Union and then Russia launched more rockets than anyone: more than three thousand one hundred in all. Now SpaceX launches more than the rest of the world put together, a hundred and sixty-eight times in 2025, to China's ninety, and it owns a third of everything in orbit. China is second, and climbing, and India, Japan and Europe all fly rockets of their own.

Here they are, side by side, at one scale. From the little Juno One that launched Explorer One, past the Saturn Five that took Apollo to the Moon, to Starship, the biggest rocket ever flown. And this is what they carried, in the order they flew. First Sputnik, then Explorer and Vanguard, and the first probes to the Moon. Then the first people in orbit, the first probe to another planet, the first walk in space, and the first satellites to carry television across oceans. Apollo Eleven, and footprints on the Moon. Through the seventies, the first space stations, landers on Mars, and Voyager One, now farther away than anything else we have built. Then the Space Shuttle, Mir, and Hubble, and the International Space Station, where crews have been on board without a break since two thousand. This century brought rovers on Mars, China's first astronaut, a landing on a comet, and India at Mars on its first try. Then the strangest payload of all: on the first flight of Falcon Heavy, a cherry red Tesla Roadster, with a dummy astronaut called Starman at the wheel. It's still out there, circling the Sun. And now, thousands of Starlink satellites, the James Webb telescope, people flying around the Moon again, and Starship. Sixty-nine years. Nearly seven thousand launches. This is everything we've ever launched.
